extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, in‑house counsel, and parties involved in patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes and analyzes the legal standards for awarding attorneys’ fees under §285 of the Patent Act after the Supreme Court’s decisions in Octane Fitness and Highmark v. Allcare, including definition of 'exceptional', evidentiary burden, examples of conduct, and appellate review standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'exceptional' under §285
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court noted that 'exceptional' was not defined in the Patent Act and therefore should be construed according to its ordinary meaning; when Section 285 was amended to include the word 'exceptional,' the term was defined to mean uncommon, rare, or not ordinary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An 'exceptional case' can include any situation that 'stands out' from another and should be decided on a case‑by‑case basis rather than by a rigid formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexible, fact‑intensive 'totality of the circumstances' test
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court held that determination of an 'exceptional case' should be a 'more flexible and fact‑intensive consideration based on the totality of circumstances.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must evaluate all relevant facts rather than apply a narrow, categorical test; the Federal Circuit’s prior rigid approach was rejected as too similar to sanction standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary burden to establish entitlement to fees
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court held that a party need not establish entitlement to fees by clear and convincing evidence; rather, entitlement must be shown by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lowering the burden from clear and convincing to preponderance makes fee awards more accessible to prevailing parties and increases litigation risk for patentees enforcing their patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Federal Circuit two‑part test (anti‑pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to Octane Fitness the Federal Circuit found a case exceptional only in two situations: (1) when there was material inappropriate conduct such as willful infringement, fraud, or misconduct during litigation; or (2) when the case was brought in subjective bad faith and was objectively baseless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court rejected treating these two situations as the exclusive or rigid grounds for awarding fees; reliance on this binary rule is an outdated/overly rigid approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of conduct that may support an exceptional finding
rubrics_metrics.description: The article cites conduct examples: willful infringement, fraud, misconduct during litigation, and an alleged pattern of 'vexatious and deceitful conduct' (as in Highmark/Allcare).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples are illustrative, not exhaustive—misconduct, deceit, or other behavior that makes the case 'not ordinary' could weigh toward an exceptional finding under the totality‑of‑circumstances inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate review standard for §285 fee awards
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court held that review of a district court’s exceptional‑case determination should be conducted under an 'abuse of discretion' standard rather than de novo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts receive deference and their factual determinations should not be reversed unless based on an erroneous view of law or evidence. The Federal Circuit’s prior practice of de novo review (treating objective baselessness as a question of law) was reversed.

rubrics_metrics.name: District court discretion and deference
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court emphasized that district courts have discretion to make case‑by‑case determinations considering all circumstances and that those decisions deserve deference on appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should recognize that district judges are entrusted to weigh facts and circumstances—strategies for fee motions should be tailored to persuade the district court’s discretionary judgment rather than rely solely on categorical legal arguments.
